segments.translation: Through understanding the meaning of [Heruka]{p-heruka}, [Vīṇāpāda]{p-vina} sets out that same meaning by way of the word '[vīṇā]{vina}':
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song: [Vīṇāpāda]{p-vina}, having understood the meaning of [Heruka]{p-heruka}, sets it out by way of the word '[vīṇā]{vina}'. The first word of the Sanskrit is damaged; the Tibetan translation reads 'the meaning of reality, the meaning of Heruka' (cp.17.m1).

flags.note: The manuscript's tavemārthaṃ is corrupt. I read tam evārthaṃ, 'that same meaning': it needs only the m and v swapped back, and it is Munidatta's own formula, used again at cp.17.m3 (tam evārthaṃ draḍhayanti … tam evārthaṃ śabdadvāreṇa pratipādayanti). The alternative is tattvārthaṃ, 'the meaning of reality', which the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) supports with de kho na nyid kyi don he ru ka'i don rtogs pa'i pi wang zhabs kyis. But at cp.17.m3 the Tibetan also has de kho na nyid kyi don where the Sanskrit clearly reads tam evārthaṃ, so its translators may have read or rendered the phrase that way throughout. The Tibetan also makes the phrase part of what Vīṇāpāda understood ('who realized the meaning of reality, the meaning of Heruka') rather than the object of pratipādayanti.

vīṇāśabdadvāreṇa can mean 'by way of the word vīṇā' (so the glossary's p-vina entry, and compare hariṇāśabda in song 6) or 'through the sound of the vīṇā', which suits a song about the instrument's sound. The Tibetan pi wang gi sgra'i sgo nas is just as ambiguous, since sgra means both 'word' and 'sound'. I chose 'word'; at cp.17.m3 I render the bare śabdadvāreṇa as 'by way of sound'.
The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rab tu rtogs par bya ba'i phyir, 'in order to make it fully understood', for pratipādayanti, 'sets out'.

segments.translit:
sujetyādi | sūryābhāṣaṃ tumbinākāram utprekṣya candrābhāsena tantrikāñ ca | viṣayacakrī avadhūtikayā saha ekīkṛtya | anāhatadaṇḍikāyāṃ lagāvayitvā bho sakhi nairātme vīṇāpādā vīṇadvāreṇa śrīherukety akṣaracatuṣṭayārtham anāhataṃ ghoṣayanti | ata eva śūnyatādhvanīti | sandhyābhāṣayā prabhāsvaram anāhatarūpaṃ sa eva bhave vilasati na bhavabandho bhavati |
tathā ca śrīhevajre —
vadhyante bhāvabandhetyādi |
tathā ca [ca]ryāntaraṃ —
bhaba bhuñjai na bāssai re apūba bināśā |
jeba biloara bāndhana bijoira melāṇā ||
segments.translation:
'The [sun]{surya}…' and so on. Imagining the [sun]{surya}-[appearance]{abhasa} in the form of the [gourd]{gourd}, and the [string]{tanti} with the [moon]{moon}-[appearance]{abhasa}; making the possessor of the wheel of [sense objects]{visaya} one with the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}; and fixing it to the [unstruck]{anahata} [stick]{danda}: O [friend]{sakhi}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, [Vīṇāpāda]{p-vina}, by means of the [vīṇā]{vina}, makes the meaning of the four [syllables]{aksara} 'Śrī [Heruka]{p-heruka}' resound as the [unstruck]{anahata}. That is why it says 'the [sound]{dhvani} of [emptiness]{sunyata}': in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, [clear light]{prabhasvara}, which has the form of the [unstruck]{anahata}. That very one plays in [existence]{bhava}; it does not become a [bond]{bandhana} of [existence]{bhava}.
And so it says in the Śrī [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}: '…are bound… the [bond]{bandhana} of being…', and so on.
And so another song of [conduct]{carya}: 'One enjoys [existence]{bhava} and is not bound: oh, a wondrous destruction! What is the [bond]{bandhana} of the world is also the [yogi]{yogi}'s release.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads couplet 1 as an imagined [vīṇā]{vina}, the sun-appearance its gourd and the moon-appearance its string, through which Vīṇāpāda sounds the meaning of 'Śrī Heruka' as the unstruck. The 'friend' is [Nairātmā]{nairatma} (selflessness personified). The refrain's 'sound of emptiness' is, in twilight language, [clear light]{prabhasvara}, playing in existence without binding; the Tibetan: it frees from existence (cp.17.m2).

equations.en: the sun-appearance (sūryābhāsa), imagined in the form of the gourd
the moon-appearance (candrābhāsa), with which the string is made
Nairātmā, addressed as 'O friend, Nairātmā' (bho sakhi nairātme)

equations.src: suna tānti dhani (the sound of the string of emptiness), summed up as śūnyatādhvani
equations.en: in twilight language, clear light (prabhāsvara), which has the form of the unstruck

citations.work: Hevajra Tantra (cited as Śrī Hevajra); only a few words are given, and the verse is not identified

citations.quoted: bhaba bhuñjai na bāssai re apūba bināśā | jeba biloara bāndhana bijoira melāṇā
citations.work: another caryā song (caryāntara), not named; I cannot identify it

flags.note: viṣayacakrī, 'the one who has the wheel (or circle) of sense objects', is obscure, and it is nominative where the object of ekīkṛtya is needed. The Tibetan (Toh 2293) has yul gyi 'khor lo can a wa d+hU tIr lhan cig byas nas, 'making the one with the wheel of objects together with the avadhūtī'. His paraphrase follows line 1b (bāki kiata abadhūtī, 'the bāki is made the avadhūtī'), so viṣayacakrī stands where the song has bāki. That is a correspondence in the paraphrase, not an explicit gloss, so I have not listed it as an equation.

candrābhāsena tantrikāñ ca is instrumental: literally 'and the string with the moon-appearance', still governed by utprekṣya. The Tibetan zla ba'i snang bas rgyud du byas te, 'making it the string with the moon-appearance', takes it the same way. lagāvayitvā is a Prakrit-style causative absolutive of lag-, 'attach', which echoes the song's lāgeli. tumbinā- stands for tumbinī, 'gourd' (the manuscript has tuṃvinā).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has gzhom du med pa'i sgra dbyig pa la sbyar te, 'attaching the unstruck sound to the staff', where the Sanskrit has 'fixing it to the unstruck stick' (anāhatadaṇḍikāyāṃ lagāvayitvā). So in the Tibetan, 'unstruck' goes with the sound and not with the stick.

For sa eva bhave vilasati na bhavabandho bhavati, 'that very one plays in existence; it does not become a bond of existence', the Tibetan (Toh 2293) has de nyid srid pa las rnam par grol bar byed pa ste / srid par 'ching bar byed pa ni ma yin no, 'that very one frees from existence; it does not bind to existence'. Where the Sanskrit has 'plays', the Tibetan has 'frees'. The Tibetan also joins the two sentences before this one: stong pa nyid kyi sgra'i dgongs pa'i skad kyis 'od gsal ba ni gzhom du med pa'i gzugs so, 'in the twilight language of the sound of emptiness, clear light is the form of the unstruck'.

Two points of construction. sa eva is masculine, so it more naturally refers to dhvani, 'sound' (masculine), than to prabhāsvaram, which is neuter here; 'sa eva … vilasati' then echoes the refrain's dhani bilasai, 'the sound plays'. The phrase sandhyābhāṣayā prabhāsvaram anāhatarūpaṃ can mean either 'in twilight language (the sound of emptiness is) clear light, which has the form of the unstruck' or 'in twilight language, the form of the unstruck is clear light'. Munidatta does not take up the refrain's ruṇā.

The Hevajra quotation is only an abbreviation (vadhyante bhāvabandhetyādi). I take vadhyante as badhyante, 'are bound', since b and v are not distinguished in the script. The Tibetan (Toh 2293), dngos por 'ching ba gsad par bya, 'bondage to things is to be slain', read it from vadh-, 'slay'. The quotation has bhāva- ('being, things'), while Munidatta's own sentence has bhava- ('existence'). A possible source, and only a guess, is the Hevajra verse ending mucyante bhavabandhanāt ('they are freed from the bonds of existence').

The quoted caryā couplet is Old Bengali, and several of its words are uncertain. bāssai re: I take it as 'is bound', with an exclamatory re; the Tibetan has 'ching ba ma yin, 'is not bound'. apūba bināśā: literally 'an unprecedented destruction'; the Tibetan has glo bur ya mtshan can, 'sudden, marvellous', and nothing for 'destruction'. In jeba biloara … bijoira I take bi as 'also' ('the world's bond is also the yogi's release'), as the Tibetan's 'ang ('also') suggests: gang gis 'jig rten 'ching yang rnal 'byor de yis grol ba'ang byed, 'that by which the world is bound, by that the yogi is also freed'.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena tam evārthaṃ draḍhayanti —
ālītyādi | ālikālivarṇākṣarāṇāṃ madhye sārākṣaram akāraṃ |
tathā ca nāmasaṃgītyāṃ —
akāraḥ sarvavarṇāgro iti |
tam akṣarasvarūpaṃ pratītya tenāgrahavarasya cittarājasya sandhir doṣacchidraguṇitvāt | ta eva pādā[ḥ], tam evārthaṃ śabdadvāreṇa pratipādayanti |
tathā cāgamaḥ | sthūlaṃ śabdamayaṃ prāhuḥ sūkṣmaṃ cintāmayaṃ tathā |
tathā cāgamaḥ | cintayācintayā rahitaṃ yat tad yogināṃ padam avyayam ||
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he confirms that same meaning: '[Āli]{ali}…' and so on. Among the [letters]{aksara} of the [āli]{ali} and [kāli]{kali}, the essential [letter]{aksara} is the [letter a]{akara}. And so in the [Nāmasaṃgīti]{tx-namasamgiti}: 'The [letter a]{akara} is the foremost of all letters.' Having understood the [true nature]{svarupa} of that [letter]{aksara}, through it he counts the joints of the great [elephant]{elephant}, the king of [mind]{citta}, that is, the holes of its faults. The master himself sets out that same meaning by way of sound.
And so [scripture]{agama}: 'The gross, they say, is made of sound; the subtle, likewise, is made of thought.'
And so [scripture]{agama}: 'What is free of thought and non-thought, that is the imperishable state of [yogis]{yogi}.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads couplet 3 through the [letter a]{akara}, which he calls the essential letter among [āli]{ali} and [kāli]{kali} (the vowel and consonant series); his paraphrase puts it where the song has sāri, 'frets'. Knowing it, he counts the joints of the great elephant, 'the king of mind': the holes of its faults. The Tibetan speaks of its 'unchanging nature' (cp.17.m3).

equations.src: gaabara (great elephant), in the comment agrahavara

citations.quoted: sthūlaṃ śabdamayaṃ prāhuḥ sūkṣmaṃ cintāmayaṃ tathā
cintayācintayā rahitaṃ yat tad yogināṃ padam avyayam
citations.work: unnamed scripture (āgama); probably the second half of the same verse; not identified

flags.note: tenāgrahavarasya is obscure. The comment follows line 3b closely (gaabara samarasa sāndhi guṇiā: agrahavara, sandhi, guṇitvā), so I take (a)grahavara as a corrupt echo of the song's gaabara, 'great elephant', and translate it 'the great elephant', as in the draft of 3b. Read as it stands, agraha-vara might mean 'excellent in non-grasping'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bza' mchog, 'supreme food', both in its line 3b and here (bza' mchog ni sems kyi rgyal po'i …). Its translators seem to have read a form of graha or grāsa, but like the Sanskrit they equate the word with the king of mind. Munidatta passes over samarasa, and over beṇi and suṇeā in 3a.

sandhir doṣacchidraguṇitvāt: I read guṇitvāt as guṇitvā, 'having counted', with the song's guṇiā and the Tibetan brtsis nas. The Tibetan construes the phrase as nyes pa'i mtshams kyi bu ga brtsis nas, 'having counted the holes at the joints of the faults'. As the Sanskrit stands, it means '(the) joint, because of counting (or multiplying) the holes of faults'.

For tam akṣarasvarūpaṃ pratītya, 'having understood the true nature of that letter', the Tibetan (Toh 2293) has de la mi 'gyur ba'i ngo bo nyid rtogs pas, 'by realizing its unchanging nature'. It takes akṣara in its other sense, 'imperishable'. Munidatta probably intends both senses, but the Sanskrit context (letters, the letter a) makes 'letter' primary. For tam evārthaṃ śabdadvāreṇa the Tibetan has de kho na nyid kyi don gyi sgra'i sgo nas, 'by way of the sound of the meaning of reality'. For draḍhayanti, 'confirms', it has bstan par byed, 'teaches'.

The two quotations introduced by tathā cāgamaḥ scan as a single anuṣṭubh verse (the gross made of sound, the subtle made of thought, the imperishable state free of both). The Tibetan introduces them once (de bzhin du lung las kyang), so the second tathā cāgamaḥ is probably a repetition; I translate it as it stands. For cintayācintayā rahitaṃ, 'free of thought and non-thought', the Tibetan has sems nyid dang bral, 'free of mind itself'. The Nāmasaṃgīti line has sarvavarṇāgro for the expected sarvavarṇāgryo.
ta eva pādāḥ is an honorific plural, 'the master himself', meaning Vīṇāpāda; the Tibetan names him (pi wang zhabs). I have not marked it as the glossary's pada ('verse'), which is a different word.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena bhāvasvarūpam āha —
jabem ityādi | karaham iti cintayā cittauṣṇyaṃ boddhavyaṃ | karahakalam iti karuṇāvahata phalaṃ prabhāsvaraṃ boddhavyaṃ | yasmin vilakṣaṇasamaye tac cittauṣṇyaṃ tena prabhāsvararāhukeṇa cāpitaṃ | ākrāmitaṃ | tasmin samaye dvātriṃśannāḍīdevatāvigrahasya | dhvanineti | anāhatanairātmajñānena prajñopāyātmakaṃ bhāvābhāvavyāpitam iti |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ | etā eva hītyādi —
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of being: 'When…' and so on. '[Karaha]{karaha}' is to be understood as the heat of the [mind]{citta} through thought. '[Karahakala]{karaha}' is to be understood as the fruit carried by [compassion]{karuna}, [clear light]{prabhasvara}. At the moment of [vilakṣaṇa]{vilaksana} at which that heat of the mind is pressed, that is, overpowered, by that clear-light [Rāhu]{p-rahu}, at that moment, of the bodily form of the deities of the thirty-two [channels]{nadi}. 'By the [sound]{dhvani}': by the [unstruck]{anahata} knowledge of [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, what has the nature of [wisdom and means]{prajnopaya}, [being and nonbeing]{bhava-abhava}, is pervaded.
And so [Saraha]{p-saraha}: 'These very ones…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads karaha as the mind's heat and karahakala as clear light, a Rāhu overpowering that heat at the moment of [vilakṣaṇa]{vilaksana} ('beyond characteristics'). The thirty-two strings are the channel deities' bodies; their sound is the unstruck knowledge of [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, pervading being and nonbeing. The Tibetan has 'the mind's camel' drawing the clear light (cp.17.m4).

equations.en: the heat of the mind (cittauṣṇya), to be understood through thought
the fruit carried by compassion: clear light (prabhāsvara)
the bodily form of the deities of the thirty-two channels (dvātriṃśannāḍīdevatāvigraha)

citations.work: an unnamed work of Saraha; only the opening words are given, and the verse is not identified

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads this passage differently throughout. For cittauṣṇya, 'heat of the mind', it has sems kyi rnga mong, 'the camel of the mind' (and later rnga mo, 'she-camel'), as if reading cittoṣṭra: uṣṭra, 'camel', and uṣṇya, 'heat', are very close in the script. For 'pressed … by that clear-light Rāhu' (prabhāsvararāhukeṇa) it has sems kyi rnga mo des 'od gsal 'dren pas na mnan par gyur pa, 'since that camel of the mind draws the clear light, it is pressed', as if reading vāhaka, 'drawer', for rāhuka. Both versions hang together. The Tibetan also calls karaha sna'i shing, 'the nose-wood', perhaps a camel's nose-peg, and says it is the mind; it calls karahakala shing bu ni phra mo, 'the small wood is the subtle'. I translate the Sanskrit.

karuṇāvahata phalaṃ, 'the fruit carried (or struck?) by compassion', looks corrupt. The Tibetan has snying rje gzhom du med pa'i cha, 'the unstruck portion of compassion', as if reading karuṇānāhatakalaṃ. That reading would also account for the -kala of the cited word karahakala. I translate as it stands, following the glossary's 'the fruit carried by compassion'. Munidatta cites karahakala where Shastri's song has karahaka.

The last sentence is elliptical. dvātriṃśannāḍīdevatāvigrahasya, 'of the bodily form of the deities of the thirty-two channels', is a genitive with no noun to govern it. It evidently glosses the song's 'thirty-two strings', and the Tibetan makes this explicit: de'i tshe rtsa sum cu so gnyis lha'i gzugs so, 'at that time, (they are) the forms of the deities of the thirty-two channels'. It may instead be meant to go with dhvaninā, 'by the sound (of …)'. prajñopāyātmakaṃ probably describes an unexpressed 'everything' (the song's saela), which is 'pervaded', being and nonbeing. The Tibetan instead makes the knowledge 'have the nature of means and wisdom' and 'pervade things and non-things'. I have kept the Sanskrit's gaps rather than filling them.

karaham iti cintayā cittauṣṇyaṃ boddhavyaṃ: cintayā can go with boddhavyaṃ ('to be understood by reflection') or with cittauṣṇyaṃ ('the heat of the mind from thinking'). My English, 'the heat of the mind through thought', keeps both open. cāpitaṃ (Bengali cāp-, 'press') is glossed by ākrāmitaṃ, 'overpowered, trodden down'; the Tibetan has kun du 'gro ba, 'going everywhere', for the latter.

anāhatanairātmajñāna could be 'the unstruck knowledge of selflessness' (nairatmya). I use Nairātmā because the Tibetan, gzhom du med pa bdag med ma'i ye shes, has the feminine bdag med ma, and because the glossary's dhvani entry reads it that way.

Saraha is quoted only by the opening words etā eva hi ('these very ones…'). The Tibetan (Toh 2293) gives different opening words, de la de nyid ('in that, that itself'), so the two manuscripts may point to different verses. The Tibetan cites the song as kA li zhes bya ba la sogs pa, 'kāli and so on', a slip carried over from couplet 3; the Sanskrit has jabem, 'when'. For bhāvasvarūpam, 'the true nature of being', the Tibetan has ngo bo nyid kyi rang bzhin.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena phalaprāptitvād ānandena vajrapadanṛtyaṃ karotīti —
nācantītyādi | vīṇāpādā vajradharapadena nṛtyaṃ kurvanti | teṣāṃ devī yoginī nairātmādikāś ca gītikayā saṅgāyanamaṅgalaṃ kurvanti | ata eva buddhanāṭakaṃ viśiṣṭādhimātraṃ sattvānāṃ samaṃ nirvāṇaṃ bhavatīti |
tathā ca dvikalpe —
yady ānandaṃ samutpannaṃ nṛtyate mokṣahetunā | ityādi | 17 ||
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he says that, in [joy]{ananda} at having attained the fruit, he dances the [vajra]{vajra}-step [dance]{nrtya}: 'They dance…' and so on. [Vīṇāpāda]{p-vina} dances with the step of [Vajradhara]{p-vajradhara}. His [goddess]{devi}, the [yoginī]{yogini}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma} and the rest, perform with song the auspicious rite of singing together. That is why the [Buddha]{buddha} [drama]{nataka}, distinguished and surpassing, becomes [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}, the same for beings.
And so in the [Dvikalpa]{tx-hevajra}: 'If [joy]{ananda} has arisen, one [dances]{nrtya} for the sake of [liberation]{moksa}', and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta makes the dancer [Vīṇāpāda]{p-vina} himself, dancing with the step of [Vajradhara]{p-vajradhara} in joy at the fruit attained, and the singing goddess the yoginī, Nairātmā and the rest. Where the song has bisamā, he has the Buddha drama 'distinguished and surpassing' and nirvāṇa 'the same' for beings. The Tibetan: the Buddha's dance makes beings pass beyond sorrow (cp.17.m5).

equations.en: Vīṇāpāda dances with the step of Vajradhara
the yoginī, Nairātmā and the rest

flags.note: vajradharapadena can mean 'with the step of Vajradhara', a dance step, which suits vajrapadanṛtya, 'the vajra-step dance', just before. It can also mean 'in the state (rank) of Vajradhara'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) takes it the second way: rdo rje 'dzin pa'i go 'phang gi gar, 'the dance of the state of Vajradhara'. I chose 'step'.

sattvānāṃ samaṃ nirvāṇaṃ bhavati: 'becomes nirvāṇa, the same (or equal) for beings'. It might also be 'becomes equal to the nirvāṇa of beings'. Where the song has bisamā, the paraphrase has viśiṣṭa… samaṃ, and seems to play on the syllables of the word. The Tibetan has nothing for samaṃ: sangs rgyas kyi gar ni khyad par 'phags shing lhag pa'i cha yis sems can pa rnams mya ngan las 'da' bar 'gyur ro, 'the Buddha's dance, especially exalted, by its superior portion makes beings pass beyond sorrow'. Its line 5b reads bisamā as dka', 'difficult'.

vīṇāpādā … kurvanti and teṣāṃ are honorific plurals for Vīṇāpāda, so I render them 'dances' and 'his goddess'. The Tibetan has de rnams kyi, 'their'. The paraphrase thus reads the song's nācanti, 'they dance', as the poet himself. devī yoginī is taken in apposition, 'his goddess, the yoginī', as the Tibetan does (lha mo ni rnal 'byor ma bdag med ma la sogs pas).

For gītikayā, 'with song', the Tibetan (Toh 2293) has rdo rje'i glus, 'with vajra song'. In the Dvikalpa verse it has gal te dga' ba phun sum tshogs, 'if joy is perfect', for yady ānandaṃ samutpannaṃ, 'if joy has arisen'. The final 17 is the manuscript's song number and is not translated, and neither is the folio number.

proposals.definition: A letter or syllable (akṣara); the word also means 'imperishable'. Munidatta speaks of the four syllables of 'Śrī Heruka' (cp.17.m2) and calls a the essential letter among the letters of āli and kāli (cp.17.m3). Where he speaks of the true nature of that letter, the Tibetan has 'unchanging nature' (mi 'gyur ba'i ngo bo nyid).
proposals.rationale: The word occurs in two segments of this song, and the glossary already has neighbouring entries (akara, aksara-sukha). An entry would keep 'letter' or 'syllable' consistent, and would record the double sense that the Tibetan brings out at cp.17.m3. Matches are limited to compounds seen here, because a bare ক্ষর would over-match.

questions: cp.17.m1 opens with a corrupt word (tavemārthaṃ). I read tam evārthaṃ, 'that same meaning' (Munidatta's formula, as at cp.17.m3), rather than the Tibetan's tattvārtha, 'the meaning of reality'. Do you agree, or would you print the Tibetan-supported reading?

In cp.17.m2, Munidatta's paraphrase of 1b puts viṣayacakrī, 'the one with the wheel of sense objects', where the song has bāki ('the bāki is made the avadhūtī' / 'making viṣayacakrī one with the avadhūtikā'). The baki entry says he does not gloss the word. Should it record this as a correspondence in the paraphrase (not an explicit gloss)?

In cp.17.m2, Munidatta's 'caryāntara' means 'another caryā (song)'. The carya entry's only English is 'conduct', so I wrote 'another song of [conduct]{carya}'. Should the entry take a variant such as 'song', or should caryā meaning a song get its own entry?
In cp.17.m5, Munidatta names the Hevajra as the Dvikalpa. I marked it [Dvikalpa]{tx-hevajra}, although the entry's only English is 'Hevajra'. Can 'Dvikalpa' be added as a variant?
For karaha I used Munidatta's cited forms as surfaces ([Karaha]{karaha}, [Karahakala]{karaha}), not the entry's 'karahā'. Is that acceptable, or should the surface always be 'karahā'?

In cp.17.m4 the Tibetan commentary reads 'the camel of the mind' drawing the clear light, where the Sanskrit has 'the heat of the mind' pressed by the clear-light Rāhu (uṣṭra/uṣṇya, vāhaka/rāhuka). Since Prakrit karaha can also be Sanskrit karabha, 'camel', should the karaha entry, or the note on line 4a, mention this?
In cp.17.m5, Munidatta's paraphrase makes the dancer of 5a Vīṇāpāda himself: he reads nācanti as an honorific plural. The draft has 'They dance'. Should the line note on 5a record his reading?
